test.title: Mini-test · The life of a city park

paragraphs.text: When the park opened in 1872, it was designed for wealthy residents who wanted somewhere to walk in fine clothes. Strict rules banned ball games, picnics and even sitting on the grass.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Over the following decades, the city’s factories grew, and workers began to use the park on Sundays. By 1910 the rules had been relaxed, and a bandstand was built for free concerts.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: During the Second World War, much of the lawn was dug up to grow vegetables. Local schools sent children to help with the harvest, and the produce was sold cheaply to families nearby.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The 1960s and 1970s were difficult years. As the city council’s budget was cut, gardeners lost their jobs, paths were not repaired and many residents began to avoid the park after dark.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: A turning point came in 1988, when a group of neighbours formed the Friends of the Park. They organised clean-up days, raised money for new benches and persuaded the council to employ a warden.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: In 2004 the park received a large grant from a national heritage fund. The money paid for the bandstand to be restored and for the lake, which had become polluted, to be cleaned.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The restoration was not welcomed by everyone. Some long-standing visitors complained that the new café and events had made the park noisy and commercial, and a petition asked for fewer concerts.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Wildlife has benefited from recent changes. Areas of grass are now cut only twice a year, and volunteers have counted more than 60 species of bees and butterflies where there were once only a handful.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: Today the park hosts around 200 events a year, from school sports days to open-air theatre. Surveys show that it is used by people from every area of the city, not just those who live nearby.
paragraphs.label: I

paragraphs.text: The park’s managers now face a new challenge. Hotter summers have killed several old trees, and the lake has twice fallen to dangerously low levels, forcing managers to plan for a drier future.
paragraphs.label: J
